title: Building a Toy Language — Tools of the Trade
summary: The practical "how would you actually build one" angle: parser generators vs hand-written parsers vs parser combinators, and where to draw that line for a real toy project or interview exercise.

slides.markdown:
Everything else in this group covered the theory of the pipeline. This topic is the practical question that comes right after: if you actually sat down to build a small language or DSL this weekend, what would you reach for, and why?

Three real options, not just one "correct" answer: a **parser-generator** tool (grammar file in, parser out), a **hand-written** recursive-descent parser (write every function yourself), or **parser combinators** (build a parser by composing small functions — a modern middle ground). Each is a genuinely reasonable default depending on the project's size, how often the grammar will change, and how much you personally care about crafting error messages.

This is also the group's practical closer, and the shape most "implement a parser for X" interview exercises actually take.

slides.subTitle: Grammar in, parser out
slides.markdown:
**yacc/bison** (and their many descendants) and **ANTLR** take a grammar file — productions written in a specification format, not general-purpose code — and generate a working parser from it, typically an LR-family bottom-up parser (see [parsing-and-grammars](parsing-and-grammars)'s shift-reduce coverage) for yacc/bison, or a more flexible ALL(*) parser for ANTLR.

The genuine appeal: you describe the grammar declaratively, and the tool handles building the actual parsing tables, including surfacing ambiguity as a shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflict at build time — a real, mechanical ambiguity check you don't get for free with a hand-written parser. The cost: you're now debugging generated code you didn't write when something goes wrong, and your error messages are constrained by whatever the tool exposes, which is rarely as precise as something you'd hand-craft.

slides.subTitle: Composing small functions
slides.markdown:
A **parser combinator** library gives you small parsers for primitives ("match this literal", "match a digit") and combinators for combining them ("match this, then that", "match one of these alternatives", "match this zero or more times") — you build a full parser by composing these functions directly in your host language, no separate grammar file or code-generation step at all.

This is a genuinely modern, code-first alternative to both the previous options: you get much of a generator's compositional clarity (each combinator maps closely to a grammar production) while staying in ordinary code you can debug with your normal tools, set breakpoints in, and extend without regenerating anything. The trade-off is usually some runtime performance (composed function calls versus a generated table-driven parser or hand-tuned recursive descent) in exchange for that ergonomics win.

slides.sectionTitle: A minimal calculator grammar, parser-combinator style
slides.markdown:
```python
# pseudo parser-combinator style
number = regex(r'\d+').map(int)
factor = number | (lit('(') >> expr << lit(')'))
term   = factor.sep_by(lit('*') | lit('/'), reduce=apply_op)
expr   = term.sep_by(lit('+') | lit('-'), reduce=apply_op)

expr.parse("2 + 3 * (4 - 1)")   # -> 11
```

Every line reads close to the grammar it implements — `factor` is a number or a parenthesized sub-expression, `term` is factors separated by `*`/`/`, `expr` is terms separated by `+`/`-` — with precedence falling out of the *composition order* exactly the way it fell out of the *call order* in hand-written recursive descent ([parsing-and-grammars](parsing-and-grammars)'s `parse_expr` calling `parse_term`). Same underlying idea, expressed as composed functions instead of nested function definitions.

slides.sectionTitle: When to hand-write, when to reach for a generator
slides.markdown:
Hand-write when: error message quality genuinely matters to your users (a production language's compiler), the grammar is small and stable, or you want full, unfiltered control over every parsing decision and don't mind the extra code.

Reach for a generator when: the grammar is large, complex, or expected to change frequently (a DSL still finding its shape, a config-language spec that's actively evolving), you want the free ambiguity check a generator's conflict report gives you, or development speed matters more than polished errors for this specific project.

Reach for parser combinators when: you want most of a generator's compositional clarity without a separate build step or generated-code debugging story, and you're comfortable trading a bit of runtime performance for that ergonomics win — a very common sweet spot for a weekend toy-language project specifically.

Three exercises show up disproportionately often as interview or self-teaching projects, and each is deliberately scoped to be finishable while still exercising the whole pipeline: a **JSON parser** (no operator precedence to worry about, but real nested structure and a handful of literal types — strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays, objects — each with their own small parsing rule); a **calculator** (the smallest complete precedence-and-associativity exercise, extendable with parens, unary minus, exponentiation); and a **tiny config language** (usually key-value pairs plus some nesting, closer to a real-world DSL than the other two).

All three are small enough to lex, parse, and evaluate (or just build an AST for) in well under an hour, which is exactly why they're the default choice for a live-coding round — they're big enough to show real signal, small enough to actually finish.

slides.sectionTitle: Over-engineering a grammar a few regexes would solve
slides.markdown:
Not every text-parsing problem needs a lexer, a grammar, and a parser — reaching for the full pipeline machinery on a problem that's genuinely regular (no nesting, no recursive structure) is real, unnecessary overhead. A simple `key=value` line format, a fixed-format log line, a basic CSV row: these are jobs for a regex or a `split()` call, not a hand-rolled tokenizer and recursive-descent parser.

The tell: if you can describe the format's structure without ever saying "which can contain more of itself" or needing to track nesting depth, it's very likely a regular-language problem, and the full compiler-pipeline toolkit is solving a harder problem than the one you actually have. Save the grammar-and-parser approach for genuinely context-free needs — arbitrary nesting, recursive structure, real precedence — where a regex demonstrably can't do the job (see [lexical-analysis](lexical-analysis)'s note on why balanced parens need a parser, not a lexer).

slides.sectionTitle: A full walkthrough: implementing an arithmetic parser
slides.markdown:
"Implement a parser for a simple arithmetic expression language" end to end, briefly: lex the input into `NUM`, `PLUS`, `MINUS`, `STAR`, `SLASH`, `LPAREN`, `RPAREN` tokens (maximal munch doesn't matter here — no multi-character operators); build a small recursive-descent parser with the precedence ladder `parse_expr` (handles `+`/`-`) calling `parse_term` (handles `*`/`/`) calling `parse_factor` (handles numbers and parenthesized sub-expressions, recursing back to `parse_expr` inside the parens); build an AST as you go (a simple `BinOp(op, left, right)` node is enough); optionally evaluate the AST directly with a small tree-walk, since there's no need for bytecode at this toy scale.

Naming each stage explicitly as you build it — "this is the lexer, this is the precedence ladder doing the parser's job, this AST node is what semantic analysis would check in a real language" — is what turns a working toy parser into a strong demonstration that you understand the whole pipeline, not just this one exercise.

slides.sectionTitle: The whole group, from the practical side
slides.markdown:
Every topic before this one covered one stage of the pipeline in depth; this topic is the reminder that the whole thing is genuinely buildable by one person in an afternoon, at toy scale — lexer, parser, semantic checks, a tiny IR or direct tree-walk, done. The gap between a toy language and a production compiler is almost entirely about the depth of each stage ([compiler-optimizations](compiler-optimizations)'s dozens of passes, [code-generation](code-generation)'s real register allocation, [interpreters-tree-walking-vs-bytecode](interpreters-tree-walking-vs-bytecode)'s dispatch-technique tuning), not about needing a fundamentally different architecture.

That's the right note to end this group on: the pipeline you've learned here scales from a weekend calculator parser all the way up to a production language's compiler, with the same named stages doing the same conceptual jobs at every point in between.
